### Location features in depth

The previous section on sessionization modeled *when* a character is online, and 
their general time-specific behavior. This section focuses on answering *where* 
a character spends their time, as character location should be a signal of whether
they are a dedicated player (focusing on late-game areas), or someone less committed
to the game.

While generating these features originally appeared to be a promising direction, 
experimental results seem to show little to no impact on the actual prediction
performance (see [Does the block earn its place?](does-the-block-earn-its-place)).
We keep keep the investigation for historical reasons, and to showcase a different
application of the `SessionEncoder`.

#### Sessionizing over character and zone

To generate the features, we use again the `SessionEncoder`, split on
`(char, zone)` instead of `char`:

```python
session_encoder_zone = SessionEncoder(
    split_by=["char", "zone"],
    timestamp_col="timestamp",
    session_gap=session_gap * 60,
    suffix="session_id_zone",
)
```

A "zone session" is the interval between the first heartbeat in a zone, to the last
one before they are seen somewhere else: this is a **visit**, not a play session. 
The two session IDs are independent and touch different columns, and a character's
sessions do not change whether or not the location features are enabled: this 
means that `use_location` can be a plain
[`choose_bool`](https://skrub-data.org/stable/reference/generated/skrub.choose_bool.html).

Visits are much shorter than play sessions, because players move around inside
a session. In March 2008, we measure ~385k zone sessions for 109k play sessions, 
and 49% of the visits consist of a single heartbeat.

This is a sample of Character 66560's session data for March 2008, where the 
10 hours cover 30 visits over 6 zones:

| zone | visits | time in zone | rarity | hub? |
|-------------------------|:------:|--------------|-------:|:----:|
| Wailing Caverns | 2 | 1h 09m 59s | 3.19 | no |
| Warsong Gulch | 5 | 30m 00s | 1.87 | no |
| Stranglethorn Vale | 1 | 20m 10s | 1.91 | no |
| The Barrens | 9 | 10m 05s | 1.43 | yes |
| Thunder Bluff | 1 | 10m 01s | 1.71 | no |
| Orgrimmar | 12 | 1m 00s | 0.66 | yes |

To note that since this is periodic polling of the data, session durations 
have some caveats. Given that a visit is measured from the first to the last 
hearbeat in a given zone, the ten minutes between one zone and another belong
to neither. Additionally, a player may move between multiple zones between two
polls and that would not be detected by the dataset. 

#### Rarity: how special is a zone

The first thing worth knowing about a zone is how many people go there. Rarity
is $r_v = \log(N / n_v)$, where $N$ is the number of characters in the month and
$n_v$ the number that visited the zone:

```python
rarity=(n_unique_characters / pl.col("unique_visitors")).log()
```

In March 2008 there are ~8,4k characters across 122 zones, and the scale runs
from Orgrimmar at 0.66 (the Horde capital, and the single busiest
place in the data) to 9.04 for the zones with exactly one visitor.

High rarity means "almost nobody comes here", and at the top of the scale it
usually means a recording glitch rather than a discovery. 
Rarity measures the data, not the world, and the
rarest observations are the ones most worth distrusting.

The bottom decile of that scale marks the **hubs**: any zone with rarity below
the 10th percentile — 1.65 in this month — is a place where everyone goes. That
is 12 of the 122 zones, and they are the capitals plus the level 60–70
questing corridors:

| zone | visitors | rarity | avg. level there |
|------------------|---------:|-------:|-----------------:|
| Orgrimmar | 4,370 | 0.66 | 60.1 |
| Shattrath City | 2,748 | 1.12 | 69.6 |
| Undercity | 2,245 | 1.32 | 45.3 |
| Terokkar Forest | 2,088 | 1.40 | 68.6 |
| Hellfire Peninsula | 2,058 | 1.41 | 64.5 |
| Durotar | 2,049 | 1.41 | 23.7 |
| Zangarmarsh | 2,027 | 1.43 | 66.8 |
| The Barrens | 2,012 | 1.43 | 28.9 |

Note that a hub is not a "max-level zone": Durotar and the Barrens are starting
areas with average levels under 30, so they are hubs only because they are *crowded*.
The list of "hubs" mixes two reasons why a zone is busy: either, hubs are where
players trade, or it's where they spend time at level cap. For this reason, the 
time spent in hubs is a weaker signal on its own than the time spent out of them.

#### Per-character aggregates

`add_player_rarity` reduces a character's visits to six numbers:

```python
df.lazy().select(
    pl.col("char"),
    rarity.max().over("char").alias("max_rarity"),
    rarity.mean().over("char").alias("mean_rarity"),
    (is_hub.sum().over("char") / is_hub.count().over("char")).alias("in_hub"),
    zone_level.max().over("char").alias("max_zone_level"),
    zone_level.mean().over("char").alias("mean_zone_level"),
    (zone_level.ge(60).sum().over("char") / zone_level.count().over("char")).alias(
        "frac_endgame"
    ),
).unique("char")
```

For character 66560 in March:

| feature | value | reads as |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| `max_rarity` | 3.19 | the rarest place they went was Wailing Caverns |
| `mean_rarity` | 1.55 | on average, a fairly ordinary zone |
| `in_hub` | 0.63 | 63% of their visits were to a hub |
| `max_zone_level` | 68.5 | the highest-level content they touched was near cap |
| `mean_zone_level` | 47.1 | on average, mid-level content |
| `frac_endgame` | 0.46 | 46% of their visits were to zones averaging level 60+ |

`max_rarity` is the one that carries level information: a character whose rarest
visit is a level-70 raid has clearly progressed further than one who never left
the starting zones. `in_hub` is meant to capture the opposite — how much of the
month was spent idling in a capital rather than out in the world.
`in_hub`, `*_zone_level` and `frac_endgame` measure the _content_ a player is doing, 
rather than their progress. 

The aggregates
are taken with `.over("char")` on the **heartbeat** table, not on the visit
table, so each number is a mean over heartbeats. Since polls arrive every ten
minutes, that is very nearly a time average, but not exactly: a visit is
truncated at its last heartbeat, so a two-heartbeat visit contributes two rows to
a two-hour one's twelve. For character 66560 the three possible weightings give
heartbeats 0.63, visits 0.70, minutes 0.60 — the same story with a different
resolution. `mean_rarity` moves with it, from 1.55 over heartbeats to 1.66 over
minutes, because the long visit (Wailing Caverns, 1h 30m, rarity 3.19) gets more
weight than its eleven heartbeats suggest.

#### Gini: concentrated or spread out

The last block answers a different question: not *where*, but *how evenly*. The
Gini coefficient over the time a character spent in each zone is 0 when the time
is split perfectly equally and approaches 1 when all of it is in one place. Low
values describe an explorer moving between many zones; high values describe a
character parked in one spot, grinding.

```python
gini = (n + 1 - 2 * pl.col("cumulative").sum() / pl.col("cumulative").last()) / n
```

Two details matter for reading the number. First, hub zones are dropped before
the coefficient is computed (`get_location_gini(..., with_hub=False)`), on the
grounds that everyone passes through a capital and it says nothing about play
style — so a character who only ever sat in Orgrimmar is not "infinitely
concentrated", they are simply not measured. Second, the coefficient is computed
per character over the whole month, not per play session, so it describes the
month's geography rather than any single evening.

Measured on March 2008 over the 5,251 characters that get a coefficient, the
distribution is bimodal: the median is 0.61, the upper quartile 0.75, and 30% sit
exactly at 0 — of whom all but 72 visited a single non-hub zone in the entire
month, which makes the coefficient degenerate rather than informative. A further
3,178 characters (37.7% of the month) never left a hub zone at all and get no
coefficient, so the left join leaves `gini` null for them. Between the two, only
62% of the month's characters have a Gini value that means anything.

**This column is no longer used.** It is still in the code, but
`make_data_op` now passes `add_gini=False`. The reason is that the coefficient is
mostly a proxy for how many zones a character visited: it is bounded above by
$(n-1)/n$, so it rises mechanically with $n$, and the correlation between the two
is 0.73. Within zone-count strata it is at chance — for characters who visited
exactly two non-hub zones the AUC against churn is 0.487, for three it is 0.494 —
and it adds nothing to a model that already knows the zone count. It also cost
1.50 s of the 1.65 s location block, because the coefficient has to run through
`map_groups`, one Python call per character, which is where polars stops being
able to vectorise.

#### The whole picture

![](images/zone_rarity.png){fig-align="center"}

On the left, every zone in March 2008 by visitors (log scale) and rarity, with
the hub threshold drawn in: the relationship is a clean straight line because
rarity *is* a function of the visitor count, and the hubs are simply the right
end of it. On the right, the distribution of per-character Gini, with the spike
at 0 standing for the characters who stayed in one non-hub zone all month.

#### Does the block earn its place?

Not measurably. Evaluated with the pipeline's own `Splitter` — an expanding
window that trains on every month up to `split_point − 1` and tests at
`split_point + 1`, with the gap month dropped because its target needs the test
month's data — the block is indistinguishable from noise. Over the eleven 2008
splits, averaged across three 10% character samples:

| location features | mean ΔAUC | wins |
|---|---:|---:|
| `gini` alone | −0.0003 | 17/33 |
| the three rarity columns alone | +0.0006 | 17/33 |
| rarity + `gini` | −0.0004 | 16/33 |
| rarity + zone level (six columns, as shipped now) | −0.0001 | 19/33 |
| rarity + zone level + `gini` | +0.0004 | 18/33 |

Every variant lands within ±0.001 of the same model without the block, and every
variant wins roughly half its splits. The per-split spread is an order of
magnitude larger than the mean: individual splits move by up to ±0.010 in either
direction. That is the honest reading — the location block neither helps nor
hurts, and the earlier claim that it was a consistent +0.0085 gain does not
survive a faithful re-run.

The Gini row is the direct answer to whether it should stay: on its own it is
indistinguishable from noise, and adding it to the six-column block does not
change that. It is not that the coefficient is useless in principle — it is that
whatever it measures is already covered by the zone count and the zone-level
columns, and the extra column only gives the model another noisy axis to split
on.

This block is also by far the most expensive part of the feature table, which is
why it is a choice at all. On March 2008 (8,429 characters, 1.22M heartbeats),
the general feature functions (sessions, monthly player aggregates, class
aggregates) take about 0.2 s, while the zone pass takes 0.21 s to encode and
0.16 s to turn into features. Dropping the Gini is what makes it cheap: with
`add_gini=True` the same step takes 1.65 s instead of 0.16 s, a tenfold
difference.

```python
use_location = skrub.choose_bool(name="location_features")
```

Code: `adding_features.py:120` (`get_zone_rarity`), `adding_features.py:162`
(`add_player_rarity`), `adding_features.py:225` (`gini`),
`adding_features.py:240` (`get_location_gini`), `adding_features.py:290`
(`add_location_features`), `main.py:203` (the zone encoder) and `main.py:283`
(`use_location`).
